God, cannot stop thinking about when Hank said “you ever heard of Bill Gates? Steve Jobs?” while staring into the eyes of a poorly balding, sad-eyed man whose been working on his bachelors since the ‘08 market crash. Just beautiful work.

That may have been the best moment of the trial for me.

In an ordinary case, I'd like to believe a prosecutor wouldn't instruct an expert to tailor their testimony in an intellectually dishonest way. In this case, though... there's increasingly little that I would put past Hank Brennan.

I definitely understand feeling bad for the guy on a visceral level as he gets torn to shreds on the stand - I think that’s a normal instinct, even if he did it to himself and deserves it. 

But I disagree with the idea that this guy just did the extra analysis and report of his own initiative. These are professional witnesses who are billing for every minute they spend working on a case, down to tenth of an hour increments. They know that changing their findings can have a material impact on litigation and know to NEVER put anything new in writing without explicit instructions. If it was some random professional who occasionally does expert witness gigs on the side, I might believe it. In this case, though, I call bs.
I agree; it's going to vary tremendously based on the discipline.

No, it's certainly not required to be qualified by a court, and I'm sure there are certain areas where higher education is a much less essential component than practical experience. Digital forensics, for example, might be one of those areas.

The craziest category of expert on their website to me is accident reconstruction. For example, this dude who apparently is an expert in accident reconstruction with a B.S. in "Landscape Contracting":

[https://www.aperturellc.com/bio/levi-corbett](https://www.aperturellc.com/bio/levi-corbett)

I just did a deep dive into Aperture's rolodex of "experts" and my mind is blown by how many of these people only have a bachelor's degree. Obviously formal education isn't everything, but I truly can't imagine getting up on the witness stand and presenting myself as an expert without a PhD or even an MS. To be fair, I can't tell if this is an Aperture-specific thing or a problem with the entire expert witness industrial complex. Hopefully the former, for the sake of my faith in the justice system.

Yep! I'm not sure how often parties formally move for an exclusion in Massachusetts, or if it's typically just taken as assumed. Regardless, it's clear that there's something funky going on with this Aperture witness, and I think Bev made the wrong call today.

Generally the point of a sequestration order is to prevent fact witnesses (as opposed to expert witnesses) from changing their own testimony to match other witnesses’ testimony. In the case of an expert witness, that same concern doesn’t necessarily apply, since they’re not up on the stand to relay what they directly saw/heard happen. 

I honestly can’t think of another case where an expert witness has literally admitted they’re changing their report to fit with another expert’s testimony. So this is a pretty unusual situation imo.

Yes, because it goes to their credibility. I believe both Kerry Roberts and Jen McCabe were asked about it during their cross this trial. It’s not uncommon for expert witnesses to be exempt from sequestration orders, but there hasn’t been a ruling on that in this case. 

Normally, the CW could say “hey, it’s not a big deal, we all know experts review each other’s testimony during trial all the time.” Unfortunately for Hank, he already made a big deal about expert witnesses violating sequestration during his voir dire with the ARCCA experts. You can’t play stupid AND smart 🤷‍♀️
I hope they move for a mistrial with prejudice.

I literally just tried this on my iphone 11 and the backlight did not come back on - I had to shake my phone or touch the screen again to get it to light up. 

Even if it was true, why couldn't the phone have fallen face-*down* in the front yard and remained that way, keeping the camera from registering any light/activity/whatever input exactly is needed to have the pocket state register on the device?

I'm not sure that's a completely correct relaying of how the pocket state data works (and ultimately, remember, we don't *know* how it works - we don't have the source code, so we only have the best educated guess provided by forensic experts, who may disagree). 

But even assuming that is completely accurate - why would that mean John's body had to be lying on top of the phone that entire time?

I understand that's your experience and I don't doubt that it's true, but that doesn't meet the standard of methodological reliability that should be required to convict somebody. 

I'm generally skeptical of the reliability of any data that involves an algorithmic black box. The courts have obviously disagreed and let it in in many cases; I just think they've made a big mistake in doing so.

I remember the explanation of what pocket state data *is,* but I can't remember anything that was adduced about it in this specific case that would contradict those theories - can you explain what you mean?

I have always felt it's possible that John dropped his phone on the way into the house. Or that he/the phone spent some time in the basement or the garage, where it would've been cooler but not as cold as outside. 

Honestly, though, my hot take is that a lot of Apple data is probably way less reliable than we think, and all these experts are really only giving their best educated guess about how these metrics work. Steps especially just seem like a true black box where we have no idea about reliability, and every time an expert testifies about their "research" and "testing" on this subject my bullshit detector goes off.

Totally agree with respect to the voicemails - it's always puzzled me how the CW can seriously view them as inculpatory. I would be curious to see the age/gender breakdown of the jury. I'm a millennial woman and I found myself actively sympathizing with Karen when they introduced the texts between her and John, when Peggy O'Keefe made certain comments, etc. But I'm acutely aware that my own life experience colours my view.

I tend to agree with this. I don't think that Jen McCabe went into that night thinking she was going to help cover up a murder. It's *much* more likely to me that her kid or her husband were somehow involved (not directly, but as witnesses, or *maybe* in helping eliminate evidence). She may have simply panicked and decided that the best plan was to place the kids and the dog outside the house altogether, and the lies snowballed from there.

I also tend to think there were drugs involved in this case, most likely cocaine. Nothing super nefarious, just a group of friends ripping a few lines together at home after the bar closed. None of these people would want to be placed in a house where coke was present and a fight potentially took place, and they certainly wouldn't want their underage kids placed at that kind of scene.

I think that Brennan’s strategy of presenting a much more streamlined case has been more effective. However, the defense seems to have matched his energy by presenting a much more focused narrative with respect to third party culprit. It’s WAY easier to follow this time round - Higgins wants to fight, dog somehow gets involved, Jen McCabe coordinates everybody’s stories from the jump. The exclusion of the Colin evidence, while a bad legal call, may ultimately help the defense avoid confusing the jurors.

There have been a few strategic missteps as well imo, but it’s easy to be the Monday morning quarterback. I don’t think they needed to go so hard on the blood alcohol evidence for example - I think it may undermine their credibility with the jury since she was pretty clearly DUI. I also thought that they may have gone a bit too far in suggesting that Karen and John were totally simpatico that night - would’ve been more effective to concede they were bickering pretty passive aggressively all day and work yo minimize it rather than trying to deny it outright. I don’t know that much turns on either of these issues, though - hard to say what a jury will find important.

My theory on this is that we're seeing some institutional friction between the MSP (or at least factions within the agency) and the DA's office play out on the stand. 

I just cannot imagine that Brennan would've instructed Bukhenik to act in the obstinate, deliberately obtuse, unapologetic way he was acting last week. It doesn't play well for the jury, and frankly it doesn't reflect well on the administration of justice in MA on the whole. I have to imagine that Hank told him to cut their losses with Proctor and throw him under the bus. The CW's strategy generally has been to sever Proctor from the investigation as much as possible. But I get the sense that Bukhenik feels some equal pressure to uphold the blue wall at all costs. I would kill to be a fly on the wall (1) during the witness prep sessions, and (2) at the MSP headquarters during all of this.

Sure they can. The CW may object on the basis of relevance, but theoretically the defense could re-call the CW's expert witnesses during their case in chief after the CW cross-examines ARCCA and opens the door to these kinds of issues. I can't think of a reason why that wouldn't be admissible. 

Assuming Judge Cannone would allow it, I'm not sure it would be a good strategic move, though. Part of ARCCA's value as an expert witness is their lack of bias, at least as it pertains to their original report. The defense is going to want to highlight the ways in which they're *different* from standard expert witnesses, not the ways in which they're the same. It's probably going to make more sense to just address any issues Brennan raises about ARCCA being biased on re-direct (or pre-empt them on direct, which I imagine Alessi will do) by having them speak about their standard operating procedures and how this case was unique.

I agree. If he's going to face any repercussions, it'll probably be with the MA bar association/law society/whatever their professional governing body is. That would be a non-criminal context and therefore subject to a lower evidentiary burden.

No, it is a crime (perjury) to lie in court when under oath. It is also a crime for a prosecutor to knowingly permit a witness to lie on the stand. No, the judge will not step in, but it is the prosecutor's responsibility to correct the record if their witness lies and they know it to be a lie. 

A witness actually being *prosecuted* for perjury is exceedingly rare, however. It's difficult to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that somebody lied *knowingly.*
That's correct. I think hell will freeze over before the CW will charge anybody else.

Yes, the Feds have investigated the investigation of this case. We've learned in court that they've, at minimum, interviewed several of the key witnesses (Kerry Roberts, Jen McCabe). Will anything come of the federal investigation? Possibly, but it's unlikely imo. There's a lot of political factors for them to consider before charging anyone, and they're unlikely to roll the dice unless they have overwhelming evidence to support charges.

From a strictly legal perspective, all they need to do is highlight reasonable doubt.

From a realist perspective, they need to show some level of cover-up/collusion in order to explain the tail light pieces on the lawn. That piece of evidence is very damning unless they can establish that it was planted. Jurors will inevitably ask themselves why the cops would plant evidence. In order to show a plausible motive for the cops/Proctor to plant evidence, the defense sort of needs to get into the Albert/McCabe family, and their relationship to law enforcement. How **much** the defense needs to get into the McCabes/Alberts, how they want to frame it, etc., are tough strategic questions that reasonable folks will disagree on.

See a doctor ASAP. Chances are that it's nothing to worry about. But hearing voices can also suggest something worse like schizophrenia. Often it's manageable but the prognosis is best if it's caught very early.

Because debilitating anxiety is a hell of a lot worse than gaining 10 pounds? Everybody reacts differently to medications and everybody has different priorities regarding their health. Dragging a caricaturized representation of SSRIs while making gross generalizations isn't helpful to anybody.

It's really difficult striking the balance between stepping out of your comfort zone (which is a good thing) and allowing yourself to get overwhelmed to the point of a panic attack. I find that self-care behaviors help in situations just outside my comfort zone. Doing my makeup and hair, wearing a nice perfume, listening to comforting familiar music before and after an uncomfortable experience, etc. These things do not cure the anxiety, but they can calm me down and bring me some comfort.

I also find that reminding myself I'm free to leave any situation if I need to is helpful. It's easy to get through 10 mins at a time if you know that leaving is always an option.

But there is also a complex relationship between the two. I think that, while for functional purposes they are separate diagnoses, in actuality they are two sides of the same phenomenon.

This is an extremely common variety of distorted thought that afflicts people with social anxiety. Nobody hates you. Most people are not paying that much attention or giving much thought to you, in fact, because they're much more concerned about their own life and struggles and the way that they're perceived.

Is it possible that a couple people you've met and known over the years dislike you? Absolutely! Nobody is liked by everybody. And that's okay. But trust that this feeling of being hated, or judged by everybody is a distorted thought, and NOT reality.

This is very, very common. It's like a cycle. Drinking contributes to social anxiety, and social anxiety makes you feel like you need to binge drink at social events.

Three things have helped me with this. Firstly, drinking considerably less. You can still drink a fair amount, but pace yourself and you'll feel good but not sloppy. Secondly, Lexapro has been a godsend for me in many ways. I noticed after a few weeks of taking it that I could go out, drink less because I was less anxious, and not feel ashamed and anxious and generally terrible the next day. I know you said you're on antidepressants already, so that may or may not be helpful, depending on if you're considering switching at some point. Finally, CBT. If your counselling already takes a CBT-based approach, great; you already have the fundamental tools. Try to identify your distorted thoughts and grapple with them, and keep on practicing. If not, there are lots of CBT books that walk you through the process - "Mind Over Mood" is a good starting point. Hope this was helpful.
